analysis.one_liner: Extends family leave, 401(k) access, and equal treatment to part-time workers.
analysis.headline: Ten senators backed the bill, but it never received a hearing or vote; it sat in committee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make part-time workers eligible for family and medical leave without first having to work 1,250 hours in a year, and would cap how long an employer can make a part-timer wait to join a 401(k) plan — no more than two years of at least 500 hours each, for workers 21 and older. It would also bar employers with more than 15 employees from paying part-timers less or giving them worse schedules, notice of hours, or promotion chances than full-timers doing the same work, and would require employers to offer extra hours to existing part-timers before hiring new staff, including through temp agencies. Workers could sue to enforce these rights and recover double the wages they lost.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time workers, who under current law can be denied unpaid family and medical leave because they fall short of the 1,250-hour threshold, locked out of workplace 401(k) plans for years, and paid less or given worse hours-notice and promotion chances than full-timers doing the same work. The bill would also give part-timers first claim on extra hours their employer has available, before the employer hires new staff or brings in temp agency workers, and would let them sue for back pay, equal treatment, and attorney's fees.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that employees work a minimum number of hours in the prior 12 months before qualifying for family and medical leave, so a part-timer becomes eligible after 12 months on the job regardless of hours worked.

Caps the waiting period before a long-term part-time worker can join a 401(k) or 403(b) plan at two consecutive 12-month periods of at least 500 hours (for workers 21 and older), with a $10,000-per-year-per-worker penalty on plan sponsors that refuse to allow participation.

Prohibits employers with more than 15 employees from giving part-timers lower pay, less notice of and input into schedules, worse benefits, or fewer promotion opportunities than comparable full-timers, and gives workers a private right of action with double damages, interest, and attorney's fees.

Requires employers to record each new hire's desired weekly hours and availability, offer available existing employees additional hours before hiring anyone new (including through temporary or staffing agencies), and compensate existing employees for hours they wanted that went to a new hire instead, with three years of records documenting the offers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with more than 15 employees — counted across integrated enterprises, chains, and franchise networks — especially retail, restaurant, hospitality, and staffing-heavy businesses that rely on part-time labor. They would bear the cost of extending leave eligibility and 401(k) participation to part-timers, paying part-timers the same as comparable full-timers, offering existing staff hours before external hires, paying existing employees for desired hours that went to new hires, keeping three years of records, and defending private lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of part-time labor, especially retail and food service

drawbacks.text: The 15-employee threshold, with franchise and chain networks counted in the aggregate, pulls in many small and mid-sized businesses that are not obviously part-time-farming operations, adding scheduling, record-keeping, and payroll compliance work on top of the wage and benefit costs.

The requirement to compensate existing employees for hours they wanted that a new hire worked, with only narrow exceptions, is the costliest provision: it converts scheduling decisions into potential pay obligations and could make some employers cautious about adding part-time headcount at all.

The pension waiting-period cap does not apply to workers covered by a collective bargaining agreement where retirement benefits were bargained in good faith, so unionized part-timers can remain subject to longer waits negotiated by their unions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains to workers are concrete and targeted at real gaps in current law: unpaid leave, retirement savings, equal pay, and first claim on available hours. Most of the 'cost' to employers is simply wages and benefits shifted to part-time workers rather than deadweight loss, though the three-year record-keeping and the pay obligation for hours given to new hires are genuine administrative and labor-cost burdens, and the low 15-employee threshold sweeps in small businesses. On balance the bill transfers income and security from employers to a large, poorly protected group of workers; the strongest honest objection is that it could discourage hiring exactly the marginal part-time jobs it aims to improve.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill with nine cosponsors on February 14, 2022.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the last recorded action of any kind.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Part-time workers got nothing. The employers that depend heavily on part-time labor — retail, restaurant, hospitality, and franchise chains, plus staffing agencies — are better off because the bill died, since they avoid the equal-pay, leave, pension, scheduling, and record-keeping obligations it would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that rely on part-time labor

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited nine Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (the only non-Democratic support).

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — after the bill was referred on the day it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All ten Senate supporters were Democrats or independents and not a single Republican sponsored or cosponsored; the bill never reached a recorded vote, so formal opposition lines were never drawn.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These are the largest employers of part-time labor and would bear the brunt: equal pay and pro rata benefits, family and medical leave for part-timers, first offer of extra hours to existing staff, and pay for desired hours that went to new hires. Their cost is precisely the income and security the bill moves to workers.
The bill names temp and staffing agency hires explicitly: an employer must offer available existing employees the hours first, cutting off a common channel for filling shifts with outside temp labor.

The 15-employee threshold counts integrated enterprises, chains, and franchise networks in the aggregate, so a network of small franchisees can be treated as one large employer — closing a common route around the part-time protections.

Forcing plans to admit long-term part-time workers adds millions of potential small-balance participants to workplace plans, modestly expanding the customer base for plan administration and investing.
